title: Left iliac fossa pain, fever and a change in bowel habit in a 65-year-old teacher
desc: This station involves a focused history and abdominal examination of Andre, a 65-year-old teacher who has just been admitted to the general surgery ward. He has had 3 days of constant left iliac fossa pain with a change in bowel habit and a fever. The candidate then interprets his observations, bloods, urinalysis and CT report, gives the diagnosis and differentials, outlines ward management (including why colonoscopy is delayed), answers his fear of cancer and safety-nets.
focus: Left iliac fossa pain with fever in an older adult: diagnosing acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, excluding complications and colorectal cancer, and managing it on the surgical ward
stem:
You are the surgical intern on the general surgery ward of a metropolitan hospital, mid-morning. Andre, a 65-year-old teacher, has just come up to your ward from the Emergency Department. He presented with 3 days of constant left-sided lower abdominal pain and a change in his bowel habit. He has no significant medical history, has had no previous surgery and takes no regular medications.

He has an IV cannula. The ED sent bloods and a urine sample and arranged imaging before he came up. Nothing has been charted yet. Your registrar is in theatre and has asked you to assess him. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Andre and perform a focused abdominal examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his blood results, a urinalysis and a CT report. Interpret them and give your most likely diagnosis and differentials. Then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer Andre's question (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Andre, a 65-year-old high school maths teacher. You are lying on the bed, keeping still, with a hand over your lower left tummy. You look unwell and a little flushed, but you are not in distress and you talk in full sentences. You are calm, a bit dry in humour, and worried underneath. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Doc, this pain in the left side of my belly just won't let up."

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: low down on the left side of your tummy (you point to the left iliac fossa). It stays there and does not go anywhere else.
  • Onset: it came on gradually 3 days ago, in the evening, and has been there ever since. You have never had anything like it before.
  • Character: a constant, deep ache. It does not come and go in waves.
  • Severity: 7 out of 10.
  • Worse with: moving, coughing, and every bump in the car on the way in.
  • Better with: lying still. You took two Panadol at home at 5 am before coming in, which took the edge off a little. Nothing else has been given since. No ibuprofen, Nurofen or aspirin.

Bowels (only when asked)

  • Normally you go once a day, formed, and there had been no change before this week.
  • On the first day of the pain you didn't go at all. Since yesterday you have had 2 to 3 small loose motions a day, and you often feel you need to go.
  • No blood, no mucus, no black stools. You are passing wind.

Other symptoms (only when asked about each)

  • You felt hot and sweaty last night. No shaking chills.
  • Mild nausea, no vomiting. Your appetite is down and you have been drinking less than usual.
  • Your tummy does not feel swollen.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No weight loss: your weight has been steady. You have never seen blood from your back passage before.
  • No pain or burning passing urine. No blood in the urine. No bubbles or air in the urine, no bits of poo in the urine, no urine infections.
  • No back or loin pain. No fainting or collapse.
  • No chest pain, breathlessness or cough.
  • No recent travel. Nobody around you is unwell. No recent antibiotics.

Past history, medicines and allergies

  • No medical conditions. Your GP checked your blood pressure and cholesterol last year and both were normal. No heart rhythm problem, no bowel disease.
  • No operations ever.
  • You have never had a colonoscopy. If asked about bowel screening: "I did the poo test once, about 6 years ago, and it was fine. I've thrown the last couple in the bin, to be honest."
  • No regular medicines. Panadol occasionally. No anti-inflammatories, steroids or blood thinners.
  • No known allergies.

Family history

  • Your father died of a heart attack at 78. Your mother is 88 and has arthritis.
  • No bowel cancer, bowel polyps or inflammatory bowel disease in the family.

Social history

  • You teach maths at a high school and plan to retire next year.
  • You live with your wife, Maria. You have two adult children.
  • You have never smoked. You drink 2 to 3 beers on the weekend.
  • Diet: "Meat and three veg, white bread. I'm not big on fruit or wholegrain."
  • You walk the dog most days.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "I thought it was something I ate, but it's gone on too long for that."
  • Concern: a colleague was diagnosed with bowel cancer last year, and you are scared this is the same. You are also worried about ending up with "a bag".
  • Expectation: you want to know what it is, get the pain sorted and be back for your Year 12 class before their exams.

The nurse and how Andre changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the admission set: T 38.1 °C, HR 75 regular, RR 12, BP 125/85, SpO2 98% on room air, alert, pain 7/10.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "He's just been to the toilet. A small loose motion, no blood in the pan."
  • If the candidate orders analgesia (paracetamol, or paracetamol with an opioid), the nurse gives it. A few minutes later Andre says the pain is about 4/10 and he is more comfortable, though still tender when pressed. If no analgesia is ordered, he stays at 7/10.
  • If the candidate orders fluids, antibiotics or anything else, the nurse confirms, and the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2."
  • If the candidate asks for blood results, the urinalysis or imaging, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • Positioning: lies flat on one pillow and is exposed to the pubic symphysis, with a drape.
  • General inspection: alert and oriented. Looks unwell and slightly flushed. Normal body habitus (height 178 cm, weight 78 kg) and normal colour. No distress and no respiratory distress. Nothing of note at the bedside.
  • Vital signs: T 38.1 °C, HR 75 regular, RR 12, BP 125/85, SpO2 98% on room air.
  • Shock and hydration: central capillary refill 2 seconds. Not sweaty at present. Skin turgor normal. Warm to touch. Mucous membranes slightly dry.
  • Hands, eyes and neck: no pallor, no jaundice. No stigmata of chronic liver disease. No supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. No scars. No visible masses, no caput medusae, no hernias. No visible peristalsis or pulsation. No Cullen's or Grey Turner's sign.
  • Palpation: on light and deep palpation of all 9 regions, the abdomen is soft and non-tender except the left iliac fossa, which is tender with voluntary guarding. Rebound tenderness in the left iliac fossa only. No rigidity, no generalised guarding. No discrete mass.
  • Aorta: not pulsatile or expansile; it feels normal.
  • Liver, spleen and kidneys: not palpable. Renal angles not tender.
  • Percussion: percussion tenderness in the left iliac fossa. No shifting dullness. Normal liver span. Spleen and bladder not enlarged.
  • Auscultation: bowel sounds present and normal. No bruits.
  • Special tests: Murphy's sign negative. No tenderness at McBurney's point. Rovsing's sign negative. Psoas and obturator signs negative.
  • Hernial orifices: normal, cough impulse negative.
  • DRE (if asked): soft brown stool, no blood, no mass, mild discomfort on the left.
  • Heart and chest: normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Andre's identity, explains the history and examination, and gains consent.
Positions him lying flat and exposes the abdomen to the pubic symphysis, keeping him draped for dignity, and asks about pain before palpating.
Acknowledges his pain with empathy, offers or orders analgesia early, and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the pain:
check.d: Score if at least 3 of the 4 sub-items are covered, including site and onset/course.

kids.x: Site and radiation: left iliac fossa, no radiation
Onset and course: gradual 3 days ago, constant since, first episode
Character and severity: constant deep ache, 7/10
Modifying factors: worse moving, coughing and going over bumps; eased a little by Panadol and lying still

check.x: Characterises the change in bowel habit: usually daily and formed with no earlier change, no motion on day 1, then 2 to 3 loose motions a day with urgency; asks specifically about blood and mucus (none) and passing wind (yes).
check.d: Critical elements: describes the current change (loose motions after a day without going) and asks specifically about blood. Score if at least one of mucus or passing wind is also asked.

check.x: Asks about systemic and upper GI symptoms: fever and sweats last night, nausea without vomiting, reduced appetite and oral intake.

Screens for colorectal cancer: weight loss, previous rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit before this week, family history of bowel cancer, and previous colonoscopy or bowel screening (one normal kit 6 years ago, none since, never had a colonoscopy).
check.d: Score if at least 4 are asked, including previous colonoscopy or screening.

check.x: Screens for complications and differentials:
check.d: Score if at least 3 of the 4 sub-items are screened.

kids.x: Fistula and urinary: dysuria, haematuria, pneumaturia, faecaluria, recurrent UTIs (none)
Obstruction or perforation: vomiting, distension, not passing wind, sudden worsening (none)
Vascular: back or loin pain, collapse, heart rhythm or vascular disease (AAA, ischaemic colitis) (none)
Infective or inflammatory: travel, sick contacts, recent antibiotics, known IBD (none)

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: no medical conditions, no previous surgery, no regular medicines, Panadol only (no NSAIDs, steroids or anticoagulants), no known drug allergies.
check.d: The critical elements are allergies (needed for antibiotic choice) and NSAID or steroid use.

check.x: Takes the family and social history: no family history of bowel cancer or IBD, never smoked, 2 to 3 beers on weekends, low-fibre diet, teacher, lives with his wife.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he thought it was something he ate, fears bowel cancer (colleague) and a stoma, and wants to be back for his Year 12 class.
Examination
General inspection: alert and oriented, looks unwell, normal habitus and colour, no distress or respiratory distress, checks the bedside.
Asks for a full set of vital signs and identifies the fever (38.1 °C) with a normal HR, BP, RR and SpO2.
Assesses for shock and hydration: central capillary refill, sweating, skin turgor, skin temperature and mucous membranes (slightly dry).
check.d: Score if at least 3 are assessed.

check.x: Inspects the abdomen for distension, scars, masses, hernias, caput medusae, visible peristalsis or pulsation, and Cullen's or Grey Turner's sign.
check.d: Score if at least 4 are named.

check.x: Palpates all 9 regions lightly then deeply, starting away from the pain, and finds left iliac fossa tenderness.
check.d: Critical element: identifies localised LIF tenderness; technique contributes but a minor lapse does not fail the item.

check.x: Assesses for peritonism with guarding, rebound and percussion tenderness: localised rebound and percussion tenderness in the LIF only, no rigidity or generalised peritonism.
Palpates the abdominal aorta for a pulsatile, expansile mass (normal) and the liver, spleen and kidneys (not palpable).
check.d: Critical element: palpates the aorta for a pulsatile, expansile mass.

check.x: Percusses the abdomen and auscultates for bowel sounds (normal).
check.d: Credit, do not require, shifting dullness, organ percussion and bruits.

check.x: Performs relevant special tests to exclude other causes: at least 2 of Murphy's, McBurney's point, Rovsing's, psoas and obturator signs (all negative).
Completes the examination with the hernial orifices and a DRE (soft stool, no blood or mass).
States the investigations to complete the assessment: urine dipstick, FBC, CRP, UEC, LFTs and lipase, and CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.
check.d: Score in Part 1 only, at the end of the examination. In Part 2, credit naming blood cultures before antibiotics or repeat FBC/CRP under item 37 or 39 instead. Give no marks for suggesting a colonoscopy now.

check.x: Interpretation
Gives a structured ISBAR handover: identifies self and patient, states the situation, and ends with a clear recommendation or request (review today, agree the antibiotic plan).

Interprets the observations: a fever of 38.1 rising to 38.3 °C that stays in the white zone, with HR 75 to 84, a normal BP and RR; systemically unwell but not septic or shocked, so no chart call is triggered yet.

Interprets the bloods: WCC 14.6 with neutrophilia and CRP 128 show acute inflammation. Normal lipase and LFTs make pancreatic and biliary causes unlikely. Normal UEC and lactate mean no AKI and no hypoperfusion.
check.d: Critical elements: raised WCC or neutrophils and CRP indicate acute inflammation, and no AKI or raised lactate. Score if at least one other normal result is correctly interpreted.

check.x: Interprets the urinalysis: no blood, leucocytes or nitrites (renal colic, UTI and colovesical fistula less likely).
check.d: Credit, do not require, trace ketones from poor intake.

check.x: Interprets the CT: sigmoid diverticula with segmental wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding. No abscess, free gas, fistula or obstruction, so uncomplicated. Normal aorta, kidneys and appendix. A neoplasm in the thickened segment cannot be excluded, so endoscopy is needed later.
check.d: Critical elements: diverticulitis without abscess or free gas (uncomplicated), and that a neoplasm cannot be excluded. The normal aorta, kidneys and appendix are not required. Credit the neoplasm caveat whether it is stated in Q1, Q2 or Q4.

check.x: Gives acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis as the most likely diagnosis, justified by at least 3 of: constant LIF pain for 3 days, change in bowel habit, fever, localised LIF tenderness and rebound, raised WCC and CRP, and the CT findings.

Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case, including colorectal cancer. Others: complicated diverticulitis (abscess or perforation), leaking AAA, ischaemic colitis, left renal colic or pyelonephritis, infective colitis.
Management
Admits under general surgery with regular observations and a fluid balance chart. Gives IV crystalloid while oral intake is poor and allows clear fluids, advancing the diet as tolerated.
Gives multimodal analgesia: regular paracetamol with a titrated opioid for breakthrough pain, avoiding NSAIDs.

Starts antibiotics because he is systemically unwell (fever, raised WCC and CRP), using an eTG IV regimen (e.g. ceftriaxone with metronidazole), with a switch to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate as he improves.
check.d: Credit any eTG regimen; doses are not required. Also credit, but do not require, stating that a well patient with uncomplicated disease may not need antibiotics. Also credit oral amoxicillin with clavulanate if the candidate justifies that he can tolerate oral therapy. Also credit blood cultures (2 sets) taken before the first dose.

check.x: States that a colonoscopy must not be done during the acute attack because of the risk of perforation, and arranges a colonoscopy about 6 weeks after recovery to exclude cancer.
check.d: Credit flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography as the alternative. Give no marks to a candidate who plans colonoscopy now.

check.x: Knows when management escalates: tells the nurses to escalate at least 2 of worsening or spreading pain, rigidity, rising temperature or rigors, rising HR, falling BP (clinical review for yellow, rapid response for red); repeat CT if not improving at 48 to 72 hours (abscess, drainage); surgery for perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis or overwhelming sepsis.
check.d: Score if the candidate gives at least 2 nurse escalation triggers with the response, and either the repeat CT at 48 to 72 hours or the indications for surgery. Also credit repeat FBC and CRP to track the response.

check.x: Plans VTE prophylaxis after risk assessment and informs the registrar of the plan.

Explains to Andre in plain words that he has an inflamed pouch in the bowel wall, that the scan shows no sign of cancer but a camera test is needed once it settles to be sure, and that most cases settle without an operation or a bag. Checks his understanding.
check.d: Do not credit false reassurance such as "it's definitely not cancer". Credit the neoplasm caveat whether it is stated in Q1, Q2 or Q4.

check.x: Safety netting

Tells Andre at least 3 specific warning signs (worse or spreading pain, shaking chills, vomiting, rectal bleeding, air or stool in the urine) to report to the nurse now, and to return to the ED for after discharge (000 if he collapses).
Mentions GP review and a high-fibre diet once recovered.
check.d: The colonoscopy follow-up is scored only in item 38; do not score it again here.

part2.lead: Here are Andre's observations, his blood results, his urinalysis and the CT report.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Andre's question. React to the answer:

  • If the candidate explains that the scan shows no sign of cancer but a camera test is needed later to be sure, look relieved. Only if they have not already explained why it must wait, ask: "Why can't you just do the camera test now and get it over with?"
  • If told most cases settle without an operation, say: "So no bag? Thank goodness."
  • If the candidate uses jargon (diverticulitis, colonoscopy, perforation), ask: "What does that mean?"
  • If you are falsely reassured ("it's definitely not cancer"), accept it at face value; the examiner marks it.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. Admission set on arrival from the ED at 09:00 and the nurse's repeat set at 10:00.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 10:00 pain score is blank. If the candidate ordered analgesia in Part 1, tell them it is 4/10 after analgesia. If not, tell them it is 7/10 and no analgesia has been given.
  • Read: at 09:00, T 38.1 °C, HR 75, RR 12, BP 125/85 and SpO2 98% on room air are all in the white zone. At 10:00, T 38.3 °C, HR 84, RR 14 and BP 122/80 are still white. He has had another loose motion with no blood.
  • Meaning: a persisting fever is a systemic inflammatory response. He is haemodynamically stable, not septic and not shocked, and nothing triggers a chart call. A white-zone chart still needs watching for trends.
  • Changes: fits ward-based treatment with antibiotics. Keep regular observations, with a clinical review for any yellow-zone value (for example a temperature of 38.5 °C or more) and a rapid response for any red-zone value.

rows.note: Admission set on arrival from ED
Repeat set: feels hot, one small loose motion, no blood. Pain score: see examiner

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 06:50 in the ED at cannulation. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 14.6 with neutrophils 11.8 and CRP 128 are raised. Hb and platelets are normal. UEC is normal (urea 7.4, creatinine 92). LFTs and lipase are normal. Venous lactate 1.3 is normal.
  • Meaning: neutrophilia and a raised CRP show an acute bacterial inflammatory process, consistent with diverticulitis. Together with the fever, they are systemic features. A normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely, and normal LFTs make a biliary cause unlikely. There is no AKI and no evidence of hypoperfusion. A normal Hb with no previous bleeding is mildly reassuring about an underlying cancer, but does not exclude one.
  • Changes: supports antibiotics. Repeat FBC and CRP to track the response. A rising WCC or CRP, or no improvement, calls for a repeat CT to look for an abscess.

handover.label: Urinalysis
handover.result: Midstream urine collected in the ED at 07:00. ED dipstick.
handover.model:
• Read: negative for blood, leucocytes, nitrites, protein and glucose. Trace ketones. Concentrated (SG 1.025).
  • Meaning: no haematuria makes left renal colic less likely. No pyuria or nitrites argues against a UTI or pyelonephritis, and against a colovesical fistula (which gives recurrent UTIs, pneumaturia and faecaluria). The trace ketones and concentrated urine fit his poor oral intake.
  • Changes: supports IV fluids while his intake is poor. No urine culture is needed unless urinary symptoms develop.

handover.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
handover.result:
Examination: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (portal venous phase), 08:05. No oral or rectal contrast.

Clinical details: 65-year-old man. 3 days of constant left iliac fossa pain, change in bowel habit, T 38.1 °C. LIF tenderness with localised rebound. WCC 14.6, CRP 128. ?Diverticulitis ?Complication.

Findings:

  • Large bowel: multiple diverticula in the sigmoid and distal descending colon. A 7 cm segment of the mid sigmoid colon shows circumferential wall thickening to 6 mm, with pericolic fat stranding centred on an inflamed diverticulum. No extraluminal gas. No pericolic or pelvic collection or abscess. No fistula. No obstruction; the proximal colon is not dilated. No discrete mass is seen, although the thickened segment is not fully assessable while inflamed.
  • Small bowel and appendix: normal small bowel calibre. Normal appendix.
  • Peritoneum: no free intraperitoneal gas. No free fluid.
  • Bladder: normal wall. No gas within the bladder.
  • Lymph nodes: a few small reactive-appearing sigmoid mesenteric nodes, none enlarged. No retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.
  • Solid organs: liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen and adrenal glands normal. No focal liver lesion.
  • Kidneys and ureters: normal. No calculi, no hydronephrosis.
  • Vessels: abdominal aorta of normal calibre (maximum 2.1 cm), with mild atherosclerotic calcification. Mesenteric vessels patent.
  • Lung bases and bones: clear lung bases. No aggressive bony lesion.

Conclusion: acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. No abscess, perforation, fistula or obstruction. An underlying neoplasm in the thickened segment cannot be excluded on CT; endoscopic assessment is recommended once the acute episode resolves.
handover.model:
• Read: sigmoid and descending colon diverticula, with a 7 cm sigmoid segment of wall thickening (6 mm) and pericolic fat stranding around an inflamed diverticulum. No free or extraluminal gas, no abscess, no fistula (no bladder gas), no obstruction. The appendix, kidneys and ureters are normal. The aorta is 2.1 cm. There is a caveat about an underlying neoplasm.
  • Meaning: acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis, matching the LIF pain, fever, localised peritonism and raised markers. Localised rebound reflects pericolic inflammation, not perforation. The CT excludes AAA, renal colic and appendicitis. Inflamed bowel can hide a cancer.
  • Changes: non-operative ward management. No colonoscopy now. A colonoscopy (or CT colonography) about 6 weeks after recovery, because he has never had one. Repeat the CT if he fails to improve or deteriorates.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Andre, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Andre now, here on the surgical ward.
Andre asks you, 'Is it cancer, Doc, and will I need an operation?' Please answer him, including the follow-up you would arrange and the warning signs he should watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, surgical intern; Andre, 65, on the ward.
  • Situation: acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis; febrile, haemodynamically stable; needs a treatment plan.
  • Background: 3 days of constant LIF pain (7/10), loose stools, fever; no comorbidities, surgery or medicines; no drug allergies; never had a colonoscopy.
  • Assessment: T 38.1 to 38.3 °C, HR 75 to 84, BP and RR normal: all white zone, febrile but not septic or shocked, no chart call. LIF tenderness with localised rebound, no generalised peritonism. WCC 14.6 (neutrophils 11.8), CRP 128: acute inflammation. Normal lipase, LFTs, UEC and lactate: no pancreatic or biliary cause, no AKI or hypoperfusion. Urine dipstick negative apart from trace ketones (poor intake): renal colic, UTI and fistula unlikely. CT: uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis (no abscess, free gas, fistula or obstruction), normal aorta; a neoplasm in the thickened segment can't be excluded.
  • Recommendation: analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics started or charted; please review today; colonoscopy at about 6 weeks.

Acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis: constant LIF pain for 3 days, change in bowel habit, fever, localised LIF tenderness and rebound, WCC 14.6, CRP 128, CT findings.

  • Colorectal cancer (must not miss): for: age 65, change in bowel habit, overdue screening; against: no weight loss or bleeding, no mass on CT. Needs colonoscopy.
  • Complicated diverticulitis (abscess or perforation): for: fever, rebound; against: localised signs only, no collection or free gas on CT.
  • Leaking AAA: for: 65-year-old man; against: normal BP, no mass, aorta 2.1 cm.
  • Ischaemic colitis or left renal colic: against: no bloody diarrhoea or vascular history; no haematuria, normal ureters.

1. Admit under general surgery: regular observations, fluid balance chart.
  2. Analgesia: regular paracetamol, titrated opioid for breakthrough pain; avoid NSAIDs.
  3. IV crystalloid while intake is poor; clear fluids, then advance the diet as tolerated.
  4. Antibiotics (systemic features), per eTG: blood cultures before the first dose; e.g. ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly; switch to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate 875/125 mg 12-hourly as he improves.
  5. VTE prophylaxis after risk assessment.
  6. No colonoscopy now (risk of perforation); colonoscopy about 6 weeks after recovery.
  7. Escalate: nurses escalate spreading pain, rigidity, rising temp or HR, falling BP (yellow: clinical review, red: rapid response); repeat CT if not improving at 48 to 72 hours (abscess, drainage); surgery for perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis or overwhelming sepsis.

• Plain words: an inflamed, infected pouch in the bowel wall. The scan shows no sign of cancer, but swelling can hide one, so a camera test once it has settled, not now, because it could tear the bowel.
  • Operation: most cases settle with antibiotics, pain relief and fluids. An operation or a bag is needed only if the bowel bursts or sepsis cannot be controlled.
  • Call the nurse for worse or spreading pain, shaking chills, vomiting, bleeding, or air or poo in the urine.
  • Follow-up: camera test at about 6 weeks, GP review, high-fibre diet once recovered; after discharge, back to the ED for the same warning signs (000 if he collapses).

ddx.for: Constant LIF pain for 3 days, a change in bowel habit, fever of 38.1 °C, LIF tenderness with localised rebound, WCC 14.6, CRP 128 and CT sigmoid wall thickening with fat stranding but no abscess or free gas.
He is 65 with a change in bowel habit, has never had a colonoscopy and has not done his recent bowel screening kits, and CT cannot exclude a tumour in the thickened segment.
ddx.against: No weight loss, no previous rectal bleeding or bowel change, normal Hb, no family history, and no discrete mass or enlarged nodes on CT.

ddx.for: Fever, raised inflammatory markers and rebound tenderness in the LIF.
ddx.against: Peritonism is localised with no rigidity, he is haemodynamically stable, and CT shows no collection, extraluminal gas or free gas.

ddx.for: He is a 65-year-old man with abdominal pain.
ddx.against: No back pain or collapse, normal BP, no pulsatile mass, fever and raised markers, and an aorta of 2.1 cm on CT.

ddx.for: His age, left-sided pain, loose stools, fever and raised inflammatory markers.
ddx.against: No bloody diarrhoea or mucus, no vascular disease or AF, no travel, sick contacts or recent antibiotics, a normal lactate, and patent mesenteric vessels with segmental CT changes centred on an inflamed diverticulum.

ddx.for: Left-sided lower abdominal pain with fever.
ddx.against: No loin pain or urinary symptoms, non-tender renal angles, a negative urine dipstick, and normal kidneys and ureters on CT.

guide:
In Part 1, Andre answers the history and gives each detail only when asked. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse reports the loose motion partway through. If the candidate orders treatment in Part 1, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2", and credit early analgesia under Professionalism. If they ask for results or imaging, say these will come in Part 2. Score item 25 in Part 1 only, when the candidate lists the investigations they would request at the end of the examination. In Part 2, credit blood cultures before antibiotics or repeat FBC/CRP under item 37 or 39 instead. Give no marks for suggesting a colonoscopy now.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods, urinalysis and CT report, then ask all four questions in order. The 10:00 pain score is blank. If analgesia was ordered in Part 1, give it as 4/10 after analgesia; otherwise give it as 7/10 with no analgesia given. Read out Andre's question to open question 4; he asks his follow-up questions while the candidate answers.

Andre is febrile with raised inflammatory markers, so antibiotics are expected. Credit, but do not require, a candidate who adds that a well patient with uncomplicated disease may be managed without them. Do not credit strict prolonged bowel rest or NSAIDs.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and the bowel change, and screens for cancer red flags, fistula symptoms and NSAID use. They examine systematically, starting away from the pain, look for peritonism and feel the aorta. In Part 2 they read the CT as uncomplicated diverticulitis that cannot exclude cancer. They treat with analgesia, fluids and eTG antibiotics, explain why the colonoscopy waits about 6 weeks, know when to repeat the CT or call for surgery, and answer the cancer question honestly.

A borderline candidate misses the bowel screening history or the fever, palpates the tender area first, or omits the aorta and peritonism. They may order a colonoscopy now, leave out the follow-up colonoscopy, or falsely reassure him that it is not cancer.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis

Andre has 3 days of constant left iliac fossa pain with a change in bowel habit, a fever, and localised LIF tenderness with rebound. His WCC and CRP are raised, and CT shows inflamed sigmoid diverticula with no complication. Diverticula are outpouchings of mucosa and submucosa through weak points in the colonic wall where the vasa recta penetrate, most often in the sigmoid colon in Western populations. Diverticulitis happens when one of them becomes inflamed or develops a micro-perforation.

Uncomplicated diverticulitis usually causes left lower quadrant pain. Patients of Asian descent more often have right-sided disease, which can mimic appendicitis. The risk factors are:

  • age;
  • a low-fibre diet;
  • obesity and smoking;
  • NSAIDs, corticosteroids and long-term opioid use, which also raise the risk of perforation (short-term titrated opioid analgesia during the acute episode is appropriate).

Uncomplicated or complicated

Complicated diverticulitis means an abscess, perforation, fistula (most often colovesical, with pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent UTIs), obstruction or bleeding. The modified Hinchey classification grades it from the CT:

  • 0: mild clinical diverticulitis.
  • Ia: confined pericolic inflammation or phlegmon.
  • Ib and II: pericolic or pelvic abscess.
  • III: purulent peritonitis.
  • IV: faecal peritonitis.

On examination, rigidity, generalised guarding or generalised rebound suggest perforation or another complication. Andre's rebound is confined to the LIF, which reflects local pericolic inflammation.

Examination and investigations

A focused abdominal examination includes:

  • a full set of vital signs and a shock assessment;
  • inspection, including for Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs;
  • light then deep palpation of all 9 regions, starting away from the pain, with guarding, rebound and percussion tenderness;
  • the aorta (a leaking AAA must not be missed in a 65-year-old man), the liver, spleen and kidneys;
  • percussion and auscultation;
  • special tests to exclude other causes (Murphy's, McBurney's, Rovsing's, psoas, obturator);
  • the hernial orifices and a DRE.

Investigations are a urine dipstick, FBC, CRP, UEC, LFTs and lipase, and a CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast. CT confirms the diagnosis (colonic wall thickening and pericolic fat stranding) and looks for an abscess, free gas or fistula. Colonoscopy must not be done during suspected acute diverticulitis because insufflation can perforate the inflamed bowel.

Interpreting Andre's results

  • Observations: he has a fever, but every value is in the white zone and he is haemodynamically stable.
  • Bloods: the raised WCC and CRP fit diverticulitis. Normal lipase, LFTs, renal function and lactate make pancreatic and biliary causes unlikely and show no organ dysfunction or hypoperfusion.
  • Urinalysis: negative, which argues against renal colic, UTI and a colovesical fistula.
  • CT: uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis, with a normal aorta, appendix and urinary tract. The report's caveat matters: a cancer can look like, or hide within, a thickened inflamed segment.

Differentials

The ones that matter are:

  • colorectal cancer, which can also perforate or obstruct;
  • complicated diverticulitis;
  • a leaking AAA;
  • ischaemic colitis (bloody diarrhoea, vascular risk factors);
  • left renal colic or pyelonephritis;
  • infective or inflammatory colitis.

Management

  • Supportive care: analgesia (regular paracetamol with an opioid for breakthrough pain; avoid NSAIDs) and IV fluids while oral intake is poor. Give clear fluids and advance the diet as tolerated.
  • Antibiotics: Therapeutic Guidelines advise that antibiotics are not routinely needed for uncomplicated diverticulitis in an immunocompetent patient without systemic features. They are indicated for systemic features such as fever, immunocompromise, significant comorbidity, complicated disease, or failure to improve. Andre is febrile and unwell, so he needs them. Patients with mild disease who can take oral medicines are treated with oral amoxicillin with clavulanate. IV therapy is used for severe disease or when the patient cannot tolerate oral therapy; Andre is febrile, nauseated and drinking poorly, so IV is reasonable, for example ceftriaxone plus metronidazole (or amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole), switching to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate as he improves. Follow the current eTG for the regimen and duration.
  • VTE prophylaxis after risk assessment.
  • Escalation: repeat the CT if he does not improve within 48 to 72 hours. Small abscesses may settle with antibiotics, and larger ones are usually drained percutaneously under CT guidance. Surgery (for example a Hartmann's procedure) is needed for perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis or for overwhelming sepsis.

After recovery

Once the acute episode has settled, usually about 6 weeks later, arrange a flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy (or CT colonography) to exclude a rectosigmoid cancer. This matters most for Andre, who has never had a colonoscopy and has not done his recent bowel screening kits. Advise a high-fibre diet and good fluid intake. The GP reviews him after discharge.

Safety netting

In hospital, the nurses escalate worsening or spreading pain, a rigid abdomen, a rising temperature or rigors, a rising HR, a falling BP, vomiting or distension: a clinical review for any yellow-zone value and a rapid response for any red-zone value. After discharge, Andre returns to the ED for severe, worsening or spreading pain, a temperature of 38 °C or more with shaking chills, vomiting or being unable to keep fluids down, a swollen abdomen, or rectal bleeding, or calls 000 if he collapses. He also reports air or stool in his urine.
points: Diverticulitis typically causes constant left iliac fossa pain with fever and a change in bowel habit. Right-sided disease is more common in patients of Asian descent.
Rigidity, generalised guarding or generalised rebound suggest perforation or another complication. Localised LIF rebound fits pericolic inflammation.
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast confirms the diagnosis and looks for abscess, free gas, fistula and obstruction. It also excludes mimics such as AAA and renal colic.
Never do a colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis, because of the risk of perforation. Arrange a colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography about 6 weeks after recovery to exclude cancer.

Per eTG, antibiotics are not routine in uncomplicated diverticulitis without systemic features. Give them for fever or systemic illness, IV if severe or unable to take oral therapy, with analgesia (avoid NSAIDs) and fluids.
Repeat the CT if the patient is not improving at 48 to 72 hours. Surgery is needed for perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis or for overwhelming sepsis.
